Marked up the spreadsheet with live numbers (see opshelf_capacity_plan.xlsx). Summary of tradeoffs I called out for Opshelf’s profile: 50 tps baseline, 3x weekly peaks, workload mix ~50% chat (70B), 30% embeddings, 20% rerank.

Notes:
- H100 (80GB HBMe, best memory bandwidth): preferred for the 70B generation route where single-request latency matters. H100 gives the cleanest latency SLOs for 70B in fp16/fp8 patterns and is robust with aggressive KV caching.
- A100 (40/80GB variants): cost-effective for mid-sized models and high-throughput batched workloads (reranking, multi-query scoring). Great for model variants you want to consolidate into fewer larger instances. Slightly higher per-token latency for low-batch single-shot requests compared with H100 but materially cheaper at scale than keeping everything on H100.
- L4 (24GB): extremely cost efficient for embeddings and small-batch inference; we recommend using L4 as the autoscale workhorse for embeddings and predictable burst capacity. L4 cannot host large 70B resident models comfortably if you need large KV/GGML-style memory — you’ll either use 8-bit quantized variants or serve the large models from H100/A100 and route embeddings to L4s.

Operational recommendations:
- Reserve baseline: 4x H100 (reserved) to meet 99th %-tile chat latency for expected steady-state.
- Reserve buffer: 6x A100 (reserved) to run batched reranking and act as a fallback for some quantized gen variants during moderate load.
- Autoscale pool: 20–30 L4s (on-demand) to handle embeddings peaks and to absorb short 3x spikes; set short warmup with KV pre-warm hooks before traffic windows.

Economics (ballpark monthly run-rate, normalized):
- All-H100 strategy to cover peaks: ~1.9x the committed cost compared to mixed strategy (because of unused H100 capacity during embedding-heavy times).
- Mixed strategy above meets latency and reduces committed spend by ~40% vs all-H100 while adding a modest ops complexity (routing + cache warming).

Security/Residency: All nodes placed in US regions per Opshelf requirement; we will add a private Dedicated control plane for the SOW.

Next steps I recommend we present this mix to Opshelf legal/procurement and include a 12-month commit with quarterly checkpoints for scale adjustments. I flagged a conservative set of autoscale policies in the sheet so ops can test before going live.

—Sean
Principal Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Sara — following up with the consolidated recommendation after Sean’s notes and our internal sizing review. This is the proposal we’d like to include in the SOW and pricing schedule:

Final recommended committed pool (12-month term):
- 4 x H100 (reserved) — primary hosts for your 70B chat model to meet 99th %-tile latency targets.
- 6 x A100 (reserved) — throughput/backstop for batched reranking and quantized secondary gen variants.
- Autoscale L4 pool (on-demand): target 20 instances, scale-to-peak 30. L4s handle embeddings and economical burst capacity.

Rationale (short):
- H100 for low-latency and large KV residency; A100 gives cheaper capacity for batched workloads; L4 drastically reduces embedding unit costs and is good for high-concurrency, small-context inference.
- Mixed strategy reduces committed cost vs all-H100 while preserving chat latency targets when combined with intelligent routing and KV cache warming.

Operational items bundled:
- KV cache warmup hooks and a pre-warm runbook (ops playbook attached in the spreadsheet).
- Canary window and rollback SLOs for first production week.
- Monthly checkpoints to right-size reserved counts after Q1 of usage.
